chapter.name: Earth as a System: Energy, Matter, and Life

questions.q: A shepherd in Ladakh depends on summer meltwater stored as winter snow on the mountains. The sphere that stores this water as snow is the ___.
questions.a: cryosphere

questions.q: A village in the Deccan has a borewell that taps groundwater beneath a rocky plateau. Which two spheres does this borewell link?
questions.a: Hydrosphere and geosphere. Groundwater is liquid water (hydrosphere) held within rock and soil of the plateau (geosphere).
o: Hydrosphere and geosphere
Cryosphere and geosphere
Hydrosphere and biosphere
Atmosphere and hydrosphere

questions.q: Over several years the Arabian Sea becomes warmer. Which chain best follows the chapter's reasoning?
questions.a: More evaporation, fluctuating southwest monsoon, uneven rainfall with floods in some regions and drought in others. A change in the hydrosphere (warmer sea) feeds into the atmosphere (monsoon), so rainfall varies from region to region.
o: More evaporation, fluctuating southwest monsoon, uneven rainfall with floods in some regions and drought in others
More evaporation, a steady and stronger monsoon, equal rainfall across all regions of India
Less evaporation, a weaker monsoon, drought in every region of India
No effect on the monsoon, because the sea belongs to the hydrosphere and rainfall to the atmosphere

questions.q: Which of these statements about Earth's five spheres is NOT correct?
questions.a: A change in the cryosphere stays within the cryosphere because each sphere works on its own. The chapter shows that a disturbance in one sphere changes the others, e.g. less snowfall leads to a lower lake level and less grass.
o: A change in the cryosphere stays within the cryosphere because each sphere works on its own
Mangroves and coral reefs belong to the biosphere
Groundwater and rivers belong to the hydrosphere
Solid rocks, soil and the Earth's interior belong to the geosphere

questions.q: Why does the chapter describe the connection between the spheres as a 'delicate balance'?
questions.a: Heating by the Sun, movement of air and water and nutrient cycling link the spheres, so disturbing one shifts the rest
o: Heating by the Sun, movement of air and water and nutrient cycling link the spheres, so disturbing one shifts the rest
Each sphere keeps a fixed size and mass, so no sphere can ever gain or lose anything
The spheres touch only along the coastline, where land, water and air meet
The spheres are linked only through living organisms, so non-living parts are unaffected

questions.q:
Statement 1: Winter snow in the mountains can end up as water in a lake, linking the cryosphere to the hydrosphere.
Statement 2: A forest belongs to the geosphere because it grows on soil.
Statement 3: The clean mountain air that we breathe is part of the atmosphere.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 only. Statement 2 is false: all living organisms and their habitats, including forests, form the biosphere.
o: Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statement 3 only
Statements 2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Fewer snowfalls in the winters of a few years can leave less grass for sheep around a mountain lake.
Reason (R): The lake gets part of its water from melting snow, and the grass depends on that water.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. Less snow means less water in the lake in summer, which means less water for the grass.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
Match each feature (column I) with its sphere (column II).
Column I: 1. Deccan plateau  2. Ganga-Brahmaputra river system  3. Snow in Ladakh  4. Mangroves
Column II: a. hydrosphere  b. biosphere  c. geosphere  d. cryosphere
questions.a: 1-c, 2-a, 3-d, 4-b. The plateau is rock (geosphere), the river is liquid water (hydrosphere), snow is frozen water (cryosphere) and mangroves are living things (biosphere).

questions.q:
Winter snowfall on a hill has been low for three years.
(a) Name the sphere that stores the snow and the sphere of the lake it feeds.
(b) State how this change finally reaches the sheep grazing near the lake.
questions.a: (a) Cryosphere and hydrosphere. (b) Less snow means less lake water in summer, so less grass grows for the sheep.
s: Part (a): cryosphere (snow) and hydrosphere (lake)
Part (b): lower lake water in summer leaves less water for grass growth, so less food for sheep

questions.q: True or False? Coral reefs are part of the biosphere even though they live in the ocean. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The biosphere is all living organisms and their habitats, so a reef belongs to it even though the water around it belongs to the hydrosphere.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the biosphere covers all organisms and their habitats, whichever medium they live in

questions.q:
Glaciers and polar ice are melting faster.
(a) Name the sphere the ice belongs to and the sphere that receives the meltwater.
(b) Name one effect on coastal cities and one on living things.
questions.a: (a) Cryosphere to hydrosphere. (b) Rising sea level threatens coastal cities; habitat loss disturbs ecosystems in the biosphere.
s: Part (a): cryosphere loses ice and hydrosphere gains water
Part (b): sea level threatens coastal cities and habitat loss harms the biosphere

questions.q: A village well has water throughout the year because of the soil around it. Classify the well water and the soil, and give a reason for each.
questions.a: Well water is hydrosphere, since it is liquid water. Soil is geosphere, since it is part of solid Earth. The two are linked because the soil holds and releases the water.
s: Water: hydrosphere because it is liquid water
Soil: geosphere because it is solid Earth material that holds the water

questions.q: Rain falls on a forest in a hill state. Name the sphere that supplies the rain, the sphere of the trees and the sphere of the soil, and say what each does.
questions.a: Atmosphere supplies the rain, biosphere (trees) uses the water, and geosphere (soil) takes it in and holds it.
s: Atmosphere supplies rain; biosphere holds the trees
Geosphere (soil) takes in and holds the water that the trees use

questions.q: Ravi says, 'The cryosphere and the hydrosphere are the same thing because both are made of water.' Is he right?
questions.a: Not fully. Both are water, but the cryosphere is the solid form (ice and snow) and the hydrosphere is liquid water. They are linked, since snow melts into lakes and rivers.
s: Verdict: not fully right
Difference: cryosphere is solid ice and snow, hydrosphere is liquid water
Link: snow melts to become lake or river water, so they interact

questions.q: A hill-station lake is much lower than usual in summer. Working backwards, give two possible causes, each from a different sphere, and say how each lowers the lake.
questions.a: Less snowfall in the cryosphere in winter gives less meltwater; warmer air in the atmosphere raises evaporation or melts snow early. Either way less water remains in the lake.
s: Cause 1 from one sphere, e.g. less winter snow (cryosphere), giving less meltwater
Cause 2 from another sphere, e.g. higher air temperature or less rain (atmosphere)
Link to a lower lake level in summer

questions.q: A warmer Arabian Sea leads to floods in some parts of India and drought in others. Name the spheres involved in this chain and explain how the same cause gives opposite results.
questions.a: The warmer sea (hydrosphere) evaporates more, which makes the southwest monsoon in the atmosphere fluctuate. Rainfall becomes uneven, so some regions flood and others dry out.
s: Sea warming is in the hydrosphere and the monsoon is in the atmosphere
More evaporation makes the monsoon fluctuate
Rainfall becomes uneven: floods in some regions, drought in others

questions.q: A rise in atmospheric temperature affects the cryosphere, hydrosphere and biosphere in turn. Describe the chain, and say how a change in one reaches the next.
questions.a: Warmer air melts glaciers and polar ice (cryosphere); the meltwater floods low-lying regions and over a long time raises sea level (hydrosphere), threatening coastal cities; this causes habitat loss that disturbs ecosystems (biosphere).
s: Higher atmospheric temperature speeds up melting of glaciers and polar ice (cryosphere)
Meltwater floods low-lying regions (hydrosphere)
Over a long time sea level rises
Coastal cities are threatened
Habitat loss disturbs ecosystems (biosphere)

questions.q: Choose a Himalayan village. Give one example of each of the five spheres in its surroundings and then build one chain of three linked changes that starts in one sphere and ends in another.
questions.a: Examples: rocks and soil (geosphere), a river (hydrosphere), glaciers (cryosphere), mountain air (atmosphere), forests and animals (biosphere). Chain: less snow gives less river water, so crops and grass suffer.
s: Geosphere and hydrosphere examples given correctly
Cryosphere and atmosphere examples given correctly
Biosphere example given correctly
A chain of three linked changes that starts in one sphere
The chain ends in a different sphere with the link explained

questions.q:
Spiti Valley's Dhar village has a grazing meadow of 10 hectares beside a lake. The lake level has fallen from 2.5 m to 2.0 m after three winters of low snowfall, and the meadow that stays green has shrunk by 30%. The meadow supports 40 sheep per hectare, and the village keeps 400 sheep.
(a) Find the percentage fall in the lake level.
(b) Find the number of sheep the shrunken meadow can support.
(c) Name the sphere in which each link of the chain (snow, lake, grass) lies.
(d) The council can sell the extra sheep now or hire a truck to take them to a far pasture at a high cost each summer. Which would you advise, and why?
questions.a: (a) 20%. (b) 7 ha x 40 = 280 sheep, so 120 are in excess. (c) Snow is cryosphere, lake is hydrosphere, grass and sheep are biosphere. (d) A reasoned choice, e.g. sell the 120 now because snowfall may stay low and trucking recurs every summer.
s: Part (b): 10 x 0.7 = 7 ha, 7 x 40 = 280 sheep, 120 in excess
Part (c): cryosphere, hydrosphere, biosphere
Part (d): a justified choice that weighs a one-time sale against a recurring truck cost

questions.q:
A coastal ward in Chennai has 12000 families, of whom 30% live on land that is only just above the high-tide line. Planners report that if glaciers and polar ice keep melting faster, sea level will rise over the long run. Option X moves the low-lying families inland at Rs 4 lakh per family. Option Y plants a mangrove belt costing Rs 60 crore that planners say would protect about half of the at-risk families but takes years to grow.
(a) Name the sphere that loses water and the sphere that gains it in this chain.
(b) Find the number of at-risk families and the cost of Option X in crore rupees (1 crore = 100 lakh).
(c) Find the number of families Option Y is expected to protect.
(d) Which option, or which combination, would you recommend, and why?
questions.a: (a) Cryosphere loses ice and hydrosphere gains water. (b) 3600 families; 3600 x 4 = 14400 lakh = Rs 144 crore. (c) 1800 families. (d) A reasoned choice, e.g. start the mangrove belt now (biosphere helps hold the coast) and move the most exposed families, since Y alone leaves 1800 at risk.
s: Part (a): cryosphere loses ice and hydrosphere gains water
Part (b): 3600 families and Rs 144 crore
Part (c): half of 3600 = 1800 families
Part (d): a justified recommendation using cost, coverage and time

questions.q: A signal travelling as an electromagnetic wave crosses a vacuum for 0.5 s. At 3 x 10^8 m/s it covers ___ x 10^8 m.
Arjun asks, 'Light from the Sun crosses empty space to reach us, so the sound of solar explosions should reach us too.' Which reply is correct?
questions.a: Sound is a mechanical wave that needs a medium, whereas EM waves can travel through a vacuum. Between the Sun and the Earth there is almost no medium, so only EM waves arrive.
o: Sound is a mechanical wave that needs a medium, whereas EM waves can travel through a vacuum
Sound travels faster than light, but the explosions are too far away for us to hear them
Both need a medium, but space has enough dust to carry light and not sound
EM waves need a medium and space has one that is too thin for sound alone

questions.q: A lifeguard wears UV-protective glasses and sunscreen at noon on the beach. Which reason does the chapter support?
questions.a: UV has much more energy than visible light, and long exposure can damage eyes and skin. UV lies between 100 nm and 400 nm and its high energy is why prolonged exposure is risky.
o: UV has much more energy than visible light, and long exposure can damage eyes and skin
UV is the part of sunlight that carries the most heat to the skin, so the skin must be cooled
UV has longer wavelengths than visible light and so it penetrates deeper into the body
UV is absorbed by the atmosphere only in the evening, so it is harmful only at noon

questions.q: Four radiations are listed. Which list runs from the lowest to the highest energy?
questions.a: Radio waves, infrared, ultraviolet, X-rays. Energy rises with frequency, i.e. as wavelength becomes shorter.
o: Radio waves, infrared, ultraviolet, X-rays
Infrared, radio waves, X-rays, ultraviolet
X-rays, ultraviolet, infrared, radio waves
Radio waves, ultraviolet, infrared, X-rays

questions.q: The clear-sky insolation at the ground (about 1 kWm-2) is lower than the solar constant (about 1.4 kWm-2). Which of these is NOT a reason?
questions.a: The Sun's output drops by about a third on the way through empty space. The solar constant is measured at the top of the atmosphere; the loss happens inside the atmosphere, not in space.
o: The Sun's output drops by about a third on the way through empty space
Gases in the atmosphere absorb some radiation
Clouds scatter part of the sunlight
Dust particles absorb and scatter some sunlight

questions.q:
Statement 1: Gamma rays and X-rays reach the ground in large amounts and are the main source of warmth for the Earth.
Statement 2: Infrared radiation warms the Earth's surface, which then re-radiates the heat.
Statement 3: Most UV radiation is absorbed by the ozone layer in the upper atmosphere.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 2 and 3 only. Statement 1 is false: gamma rays and X-rays are mostly filtered by the upper atmosphere, and about 99% of the Sun's energy is UV, visible and infrared.
o: Statements 2 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
All three statements

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The solar constant is the energy received per unit area at the Earth's surface under a clear sky.
Reason (R): Gases, clouds and dust absorb and scatter some sunlight on its way down.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true. The solar constant is the energy at the top of the atmosphere, before any absorption or scattering.
o: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

questions.q: A school fits a 2 m2 panel on its roof. If the insolation is 1 kWm-2 for 30 minutes, the energy falling on the panel is

(a) Name the atlas published in 1982 on India's sunshine and its two authors.
(b) Give the reason the chapter offers for India's large solar potential.
questions.a: (a) Solar Radiation Over India, by Anna Mani and S. Rangarajan. (b) India lies in the tropical and sub-tropical regions and receives abundant sunlight throughout the year.
s: Part (a): Solar Radiation Over India by Anna Mani and S. Rangarajan
Part (b): tropical and sub-tropical location gives abundant sunlight all year

questions.q: True or False? Sunlight, like sound, needs air to reach the Earth. Give the verdict and the correction.
questions.a: False. Sunlight is an EM wave and travels through a vacuum at the speed of light; sound is a mechanical wave that needs a medium.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: EM waves need no medium, while sound waves do

questions.q:
A 3 m2 panel receives an insolation of 1 kWm-2 for one hour.
(a) Find the energy falling on it in joules.
(b) Express this in units of household electricity (1 unit = 3.6 x 10^6 J).
s: Part (a): E = intensity x area x time = 1.08 x 10^7 J
Part (b): 3 units

questions.q: Gamma rays and X-rays carry very high energy and can harm life, yet people on the ground are not harmed by those from the Sun. Explain.
questions.a: These rays are mostly filtered out by the Earth's upper atmosphere, and the Sun's energy reaching Earth is mainly UV, visible and infrared.
s: Gamma rays and X-rays are mostly filtered by the upper atmosphere
About 99% of solar energy reaching Earth is UV, visible and infrared

questions.q: State one effect on the Earth of the Sun's ultraviolet radiation and one effect of its infrared radiation.
questions.a: UV is mostly absorbed by the ozone layer, which protects life and heats the upper atmosphere. Infrared warms the Earth's surface.
s: UV: absorbed by the ozone layer, protecting life and heating the upper atmosphere
Infrared warms the Earth's surface

questions.q: Sunita claims, 'Microwaves and radio waves from the Sun do not warm the Earth because they never reach it.' Is she right?
questions.a: Her reason is wrong. These waves do arrive, but they carry very little energy, so they cannot warm the Earth significantly.
s: Verdict: the claim's reason is wrong
They do reach the Earth, since all EM waves travel through a vacuum
They carry too little energy to warm it significantly

questions.q: Show that 5.0 x 10^6 J cannot fall on 1 m2 of the ground in one hour on a clear day, and say where such an amount could be received.
questions.a: At the ground the maximum is about 1 kWm-2, so one hour gives 3.6 x 10^6 J, below 5.0 x 10^6 J. At the top of the atmosphere (1.4 kWm-2) it is 5.04 x 10^6 J, so only there.
s: Clear-sky ground insolation is about 1 kWm-2, giving 3.6 x 10^6 J in an hour
5.0 x 10^6 J is larger than this, so it cannot fall on the ground
Solar constant 1.4 kWm-2 gives 5.04 x 10^6 J at the top of the atmosphere

questions.q: Describe what happens to the Sun's ultraviolet, visible and infrared radiation on reaching the Earth, one effect for each.
questions.a: UV is mostly absorbed by the ozone layer. Visible light reaches the surface, powers photosynthesis and partly warms land and water. Infrared warms the surface, which re-radiates heat that greenhouse gases partly trap.
s: UV is mostly absorbed by the ozone layer
Visible light powers photosynthesis and partly warms land and water
Infrared warms the surface, which re-radiates heat that greenhouse gases trap

questions.q: Follow the Sun's infrared radiation from the Sun to space. Describe each stage, naming the surface, the re-radiation and the gases involved, and say why the Earth would be too cold without the last stage.
questions.a: Infrared reaches and warms the Earth's surface; the warm surface re-radiates heat back into the atmosphere; greenhouse gases (CO2, methane, water vapour) trap a portion; this keeps the Earth warm. Without this trapping, heat would escape and the Earth would be too cold for life.
s: Infrared from the Sun reaches and warms the Earth's surface
The warm surface re-radiates heat into the atmosphere
Greenhouse gases CO2, CH4 and water vapour trap a portion of it
The trapped heat keeps the Earth warm enough for life
Without trapping the heat escapes and the Earth is too cold for life

questions.q: Distinguish the solar constant from insolation. Find the energy one square metre receives in one hour in each case (take 1.4 kWm-2 and 1 kWm-2), the difference as a percentage of the first, and give the reasons for the difference.
questions.a: Solar constant: energy per unit area at the top of the atmosphere (1.4 kWm-2), 5.04 x 10^6 J in an hour. Insolation: radiation reaching the surface (about 1 kWm-2 clear sky), 3.6 x 10^6 J. Difference 1.44 x 10^6 J, about 28.6%, because gases, clouds and dust absorb and scatter sunlight.
s: Solar constant: energy at the top of the atmosphere before absorption; insolation: radiation reaching the surface
5.04 x 10^6 J for the solar constant in one hour
3.6 x 10^6 J for the insolation in one hour
Difference 1.44 x 10^6 J, about 28.6%
Reason: gases, clouds and dust absorb and scatter some of it

questions.q:
A school wants to meet its need of 120 units of electricity a day from the Sun. Its roof can hold 40 m2 of panels. Take insolation as 1 kWm-2 for 5 hours a day, 1 unit = 3.6 x 10^6 J, and assume the panels turn 20% of the energy falling on them into electricity. More panels cost Rs 6000 per m2, and units bought from the grid cost Rs 8 each.
(a) Find the energy falling on the 40 m2 roof in a day, in joules.
(b) Express it in units.
(c) Find the units of electricity produced and the daily shortfall.
(d) The school can add panels over the parking area to cover the whole shortfall or buy the shortfall from the grid. Which would you advise, and why?
questions.a: (a) 7.2 x 10^8 J. (b) 200 units. (c) 20% of 200 = 40 units, shortfall 80 units. (d) 80 m2 more costs Rs 4.8 lakh and saves Rs 640 a day, repaid in 750 days, about two years; advise adding panels, with the grid as backup on cloudy days.
s: Part (b): 200 units
Part (c): 40 units produced and 80 units short
Part (d): a justified choice that uses the cost and the payback period

questions.q:
Two villages measure the insolation at noon. Jaisalmer, on a clear day, reads 0.95 kWm-2. Shillong, under thick cloud, reads 0.40 kWm-2. The solar constant is 1.4 kWm-2. A community hall needs panels to give the same energy as 20 m2 in Jaisalmer, and panels cost Rs 6000 per m2.
(a) Find the percentage of the solar constant reaching the ground in each place.
(b) Find the energy falling on 2 m2 in two hours in each place.
(c) Name the cause of the lower reading at Shillong.
(d) Find the area of panels needed at Shillong and its cost, and say whether solar power is still a sensible choice there.
questions.a: (a) 67.9% and 28.6%. (b) 1.368 x 10^7 J and 5.76 x 10^6 J. (c) Clouds (with gases and dust) absorb and scatter sunlight before it reaches the ground. (d) 20 x 0.95/0.40 = 47.5 m2, costing Rs 2.85 lakh against Rs 1.2 lakh; a reasoned view, e.g. still sensible if the grid is unreliable, but needs far more panels.
s: Part (a): 67.9% in Jaisalmer and 28.6% in Shillong
Part (c): clouds, with gases and dust, absorb and scatter sunlight
Part (d): 47.5 m2, Rs 2.85 lakh, with a justified judgement

questions.q: Snow of albedo 0.85 reflects most sunlight. Out of every 1000 J of sunlight falling on it, the snow absorbs ___ J.
Using the albedo values in Table 13.1 (snow 0.80-0.90, ice 0.50-0.70, crushed rock 0.25-0.30), which surface absorbs the largest share of the sunlight falling on it?
questions.a: Crushed rock. The lowest albedo means the least reflection and so the most absorption.
o: Crushed rock
Ice
Snow
Fresh snow and ice absorb equally, since both are frozen water

questions.q: On a hot summer night Meena feels the room of a concrete house is hotter than the thick-walled mud house of her grandmother. What explains this?
questions.a: Concrete absorbs heat in the day and re-radiates it at night, whereas thick mud and wood re-radiate less. All objects radiate heat, and the concrete's re-radiation is large.
o: Concrete absorbs heat in the day and re-radiates it at night, whereas thick mud and wood re-radiate less
Mud walls reflect all the sunlight, so they never become warm during the day
Concrete creates heat at night through chemical reactions with the air
Mud houses stand at a higher latitude and so receive less sunlight than concrete houses

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a reason why a city is warmer than the farmland around it?
questions.a: Cities lie nearer the Sun, so they receive stronger sunlight at the top of the atmosphere. The urban heat island effect comes from how land is used, not from the city being closer to the Sun.
o: Cities lie nearer the Sun, so they receive stronger sunlight at the top of the atmosphere
Steel, concrete, brick and asphalt absorb and retain heat
Built-up materials re-radiate the heat they have stored
Cities have less vegetation to give shade and transpire water

questions.q: Equal beams of sunlight fall on the equator and near a pole. Why do the equatorial regions stay relatively warm all year?
questions.a: The radiation is concentrated over a smaller area at the equator and spread over a larger area near the pole. The Earth is spherical, so the Sun's rays strike different latitudes at different angles.
o: The radiation is concentrated over a smaller area at the equator and spread over a larger area near the pole
The equator is closer to the Sun than the poles, so its rays are stronger
The poles receive no sunlight in any season, so only the equator is warmed
The atmosphere over the equator absorbs all the sunlight and turns it to heat

questions.q:
Statement 1: Snow has an albedo of about 0.80-0.90, so it reflects most incoming sunlight.
Statement 2: Albedo is the amount of heat that a surface re-radiates at night.
Statement 3: Near the poles sunlight is spread over a smaller area than at the equator.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 only. Statement 2 is false: albedo is the fraction of solar radiation reflected. Statement 3 is false: near the poles the sunlight is spread over a larger area.
o: Statement 1 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A dark-coloured road heats up more quickly in the sun than a light-coloured surface.
Reason (R): Dark surfaces have a high albedo.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false. Dark surfaces have a low albedo: they reflect little and absorb more sunlight.
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
Match each item (column I) with its description (column II).
Column I: 1. Snow  2. Black soil  3. Steel and concrete city  4. Equatorial region
Column II: a. low albedo, warms quickly  b. high albedo, stays cool  c. absorbs and re-radiates heat, forming a heat island  d. sunlight concentrated over a smaller area
questions.a: 1-b, 2-a, 3-c, 4-d. Snow has a high albedo, black soil a low albedo, the built-up city holds heat, and the equator gets concentrated rays.

questions.q:
(a) Define albedo.
(b) Give two reasons why the polar regions stay very cold.
questions.a: (a) Albedo is the fraction of solar radiation reflected by a surface. (b) Snow and ice have high albedo and reflect most sunlight, and near the poles the Sun's radiation is spread over a larger area.
s: Part (a): fraction of solar radiation reflected by a surface
Part (b): high albedo of snow and ice, and radiation spread over a larger area at high latitude

questions.q: True or False? A surface with albedo 0.9 absorbs more sunlight than a surface with albedo 0.3. Give the verdict and the correction.
questions.a: False. A high albedo means more is reflected; the surface of albedo 0.9 absorbs only 10% and the surface of 0.3 absorbs 70%.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: higher albedo means more reflection and less absorption (10% against 70%)

questions.q:
Sunlight of 1000 J per second falls on each square metre of snow (albedo 0.85) and of crushed rock (albedo 0.25).
(a) Find the energy absorbed per second by 1 m2 of each.
(b) Say how many times more the crushed rock absorbs.
questions.a: (a) Snow absorbs 150 J/s and crushed rock 750 J/s. (b) 750/150 = 5 times as much.
s: Part (a): 150 J/s for snow and 750 J/s for crushed rock
Part (b): 5 times

questions.q: Explain why a city centre stays warmer than the surrounding countryside even after sunset.
questions.a: Steel, concrete, brick and asphalt absorb and retain heat in the day and re-radiate it after dark, while rural areas with plants cool down by shade and transpiration.
s: Built materials absorb and retain heat and re-radiate it at night
Rural areas and forests lose heat through shade and plant transpiration

questions.q: A forest patch beside a town is cooler than the town at midday. Give two features of the forest that explain this.
questions.a: The trees give shade, and plants lose water by transpiration, which cools the surroundings.
s: Shade from the trees
Transpiration by plants cools the air

questions.q: Neha says, 'Equatorial regions stay warm because the equator is nearer to the Sun than the poles.' Is her reason correct?
questions.a: No. The reason is the spherical shape of the Earth: the rays strike the equator more directly, so the radiation is concentrated over a smaller area, while near the poles it is spread over a larger area.
s: Verdict: reason is not correct
Real reason: the Earth is spherical so rays strike different latitudes at different angles
Radiation is concentrated over a smaller area at the equator and spread over a larger area near the poles

questions.q: A tin roof stays much cooler after being painted. Working backwards, state what has changed in its albedo, how the roof treats sunlight now and what is the colour change likely to be.
questions.a: Its albedo has risen. More sunlight is reflected and less absorbed, so the roof heats up less. The paint was probably changed from a dark colour to a light one.
s: The albedo of the roof has increased
More sunlight is reflected and less is absorbed
The colour changed from dark to light

questions.q: A city wants to reduce its heat island effect. Suggest three measures, each linked to a cause given in the chapter.
questions.a: Use light-coloured (high albedo) roofs and roads to reflect more sunlight; plant trees to give shade and add transpiration; reduce the heat-retaining built surfaces that re-radiate heat at night.
s: Light-coloured roofs or roads for higher albedo
More trees and plants for shade and transpiration
Less heat-retaining built material, which re-radiates at night

questions.q: Explain how the shape of the Earth and its latitude lead to uneven heating, and say what the uneven heating finally drives. Include the role of the tilt of the axis.
questions.a: The Earth is spherical, so rays strike different latitudes at different angles; at the equator radiation is concentrated over a smaller area and at the poles spread over a larger area, so the equator is warm and the poles cold. Tilt of the axis gives seasons and changing day length. This uneven heating drives global winds and ocean currents.
s: Spherical Earth: rays strike different latitudes at different angles
Equator: radiation concentrated over a smaller area
Poles: radiation spread over a larger area, so the temperature difference
Tilt of the axis gives seasons and changing length of day
Uneven heating drives global winds and ocean currents

questions.q: Compare a dark-roofed colony with a snow-covered valley using albedo. Explain, with the albedo values from the chapter, which absorbs more, why, what that means for the temperatures, and how the melting of snow would change this.
questions.a: Dark roofs (low albedo) absorb most sunlight; snow (0.80-0.90) reflects most and stays cool. Crushed rock (0.25-0.30) is exposed after snow melts, so it absorbs about five times as much as snow does. So the melting itself speeds warming.
s: Dark roofs have a low albedo and absorb more sunlight
Snow has an albedo of 0.80-0.90 and reflects most sunlight
Result: the colony warms faster and snow stays cool
Bare crushed rock (0.25-0.30) absorbs far more than snow
So melting exposes darker ground and increases warming

questions.q:
A school in Jaipur has a 200 m2 flat roof. At noon the sunlight falling on it is 900 J per second per m2. A dark roof coating has albedo 0.2 and a white coating has albedo 0.7. White paint costs Rs 60 per m2 and needs repainting every year because dust darkens it.
(a) Find the energy absorbed per second by the whole roof with each coating.
(b) Find the energy saved per hour by white paint, in joules and in units (1 unit = 3.6 x 10^6 J).
(c) Find the cost of painting the roof white.
(d) The school can paint white each year or leave the dark roof and run extra air conditioning. Which is better, and why?
questions.a: (a) Dark: 0.8 x 900 x 200 = 144000 J/s; white: 0.3 x 900 x 200 = 54000 J/s. (b) 90000 J/s x 3600 = 3.24 x 10^8 J = 90 units. (c) Rs 12000. (d) A justified choice, e.g. paint white: Rs 12000 a year is small against 90 units of heat a noon hour, though dust lowers the benefit so repaint yearly.
s: Part (a): 144000 J/s and 54000 J/s
Part (b): 3.24 x 10^8 J, i.e. 90 units
Part (d): a justified choice that weighs the small cost, the yearly repainting and the benefit

questions.q:
On a summer night at 11 pm, a thermometer in a city centre reads 33.5 C, in the farmland outside it 29.0 C and in a forest 27.5 C. The council estimates that each 1 C of extra night heat raises air-conditioning demand by 6%. In a pilot ward, planting 20000 trees at Rs 500 each lowered the night temperature by 1.2 C, and white roofs costing Rs 40 lakh lowered it by 0.8 C.
(a) Find the city's excess over farmland and over forest.
(b) Find the percentage rise in air-conditioning demand because of the excess over farmland.
(c) Find the cost per degree of cooling for trees and for roofs, in crore rupees.
(d) Name the cause of the difference and advise the council on what to do.
questions.a: (a) 4.5 C and 6.0 C. (b) 4.5 x 6 = 27%. (c) Trees Rs 1 crore for 1.2 C = Rs 0.83 crore per C; roofs Rs 0.4 crore for 0.8 C = Rs 0.5 crore per C. (d) Built materials absorb and re-radiate heat (urban heat island) while farmland and forest cool by shade and transpiration; a justified plan, e.g. roofs first for lowest cost per degree, with trees added for shade.
s: Part (a): 4.5 C over farmland and 6.0 C over forest
Part (b): 27%
Part (c): about Rs 0.83 crore per C for trees and Rs 0.5 crore per C for roofs
Part (d): urban heat island cause and a justified plan using cost and other benefits

questions.q: The air in a valley is at 30 C. At the rate given in the chapter (6.5 C per km), the air on a ridge 4 km higher in the troposphere is at ___ C.
Passengers on a flight find that above the storm clouds the air is smooth and calm. Which reasoning matches the chapter?
questions.a: In the stratosphere the temperature rises with height, so there is little vertical mixing and weather stays below. Ozone absorbs UV and warms the stratosphere, which calms it and confines weather to the troposphere.
o: In the stratosphere the temperature rises with height, so there is little vertical mixing and weather stays below
Storms stop because the stratosphere has no air at all
The stratosphere is colder than the troposphere, so clouds cannot form there
Winds blow faster in the stratosphere and so push the clouds back down

questions.q: Venus is hotter than Mercury although Mercury is closer to the Sun. What is the best explanation?
questions.a: The atmosphere of Venus has caused an uncontrolled greenhouse effect. Heat is trapped by the atmosphere of Venus, whereas Mercury has no such atmosphere.
o: The atmosphere of Venus has caused an uncontrolled greenhouse effect
Venus has a thicker ozone layer, which makes it warmer
Mercury reflects all the sunlight that reaches it, but Venus reflects none
Venus is larger, so it receives more sunlight per unit area than Mercury

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a role of the atmosphere in protecting life on Earth?
questions.a: It stops all the infrared heat from the surface leaving, so the Earth never loses any heat. Greenhouse gases trap only a portion of the outgoing heat; the rest escapes to space.
o: It stops all the infrared heat from the surface leaving, so the Earth never loses any heat
The ozone layer blocks harmful UV rays
Clouds and gases absorb some sunlight before it reaches the surface
Greenhouse gases trap part of the heat re-radiated by the surface

questions.q: Dev says, 'Ozone is a protective gas, so the ozone in city smog must be good for us.' Which reply is right?
questions.a: Ozone high in the stratosphere blocks UV, but ground-level ozone formed from vehicle emissions and sunlight is harmful to health. The same gas helps at one height and harms at another.
o: Ozone high in the stratosphere blocks UV, but ground-level ozone formed from vehicle emissions and sunlight is harmful to health
Ozone is harmful everywhere, so the stratospheric ozone layer should be removed
Ground-level ozone is made by CFCs and is the same as the ozone hole
Ozone is protective at every height and smog only makes it stronger

questions.q:
Statement 1: Almost all weather occurs in the troposphere.
Statement 2: The ozone layer lies in the stratosphere.
Statement 3: In the stratosphere the temperature decreases with height at about 6.5 C per km.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 2 only. Statement 3 is false: in the stratosphere the temperature rises with height because ozone absorbs UV.
o: Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 1 only
All three statements

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Without the atmosphere the Earth would be too cold for life.
Reason (R): Greenhouse gases absorb the heat re-radiated by the surface and prevent it from escaping into space.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. Trapping of outgoing heat keeps the surface warm enough for life.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: Plants need carbon dioxide, so why does the chapter call an excess of it undesirable?
questions.a: Some CO2 keeps the Earth warm, but too much intensifies the greenhouse effect and causes global warming. The balance is critical: enough CO2 supports life, too much heats the planet.
o: Some CO2 keeps the Earth warm, but too much intensifies the greenhouse effect and causes global warming
CO2 is a poison for plants as soon as its amount rises above 1%
Excess CO2 removes the ozone layer in the stratosphere
Excess CO2 stops the surface from re-radiating any heat at all

questions.q:
(a) Where is the troposphere tallest and where is it lowest?
(b) Why is weather confined to the troposphere?
questions.a: (a) Tallest above the equator and lowest above the polar regions. (b) The temperature rises with height in the stratosphere, which calms it by stopping vertical mixing, so weather stays in the troposphere.
s: Part (a): tallest above the equator, lowest above the poles
Part (b): the rising temperature in the stratosphere stops vertical mixing of air

questions.q: True or False? In the stratosphere the temperature rises with height because ozone absorbs UV. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Ozone absorbs ultraviolet rays and heats the surrounding air, so the temperature increases with height.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: ozone absorbs UV rays and heats the air

questions.q:
On a day the air at the ground is 30 C, an aircraft climbs to 10 km, still in the troposphere.
(a) Find the outside temperature at 10 km, using 6.5 C per km.
(b) State what happens to the temperature once the plane goes above 12 km into the stratosphere, and why.
questions.a: (a) 30 - 65 = -35 C. (b) It begins to rise with height, as the ozone layer absorbs UV.
s: Part (b): temperature rises in the stratosphere because ozone absorbs UV

questions.q: State the two ways in which the atmosphere protects life on Earth.
questions.a: It partly absorbs incoming solar radiation (ozone blocks UV, clouds and gases absorb some sunlight), and it traps outgoing heat through greenhouse gases such as CO2, methane and water vapour.
s: Absorbs part of the incoming radiation, e.g. UV by ozone
Traps outgoing heat with greenhouse gases

questions.q: Name the chemicals that caused the ozone hole over Antarctica, two things they were used in, and the agreement that helped the layer recover.
questions.a: CFCs, used in refrigerators and aerosols; the Montreal Protocol reduced their use and the layer is slowly recovering.
s: CFCs used in refrigerators and aerosols
Montreal Protocol reduced their use and the ozone layer is slowly recovering

questions.q: Karan says, 'Greenhouse gases are harmful, so the Earth would be better off with none.' Is he right?
questions.a: No. Greenhouse gases trap part of the heat re-radiated by the surface; without that, the Earth would be too cold for life. Only the excess of CO2 from human activity is harmful.
s: Verdict: not right
Without greenhouse gases the heat escapes and the Earth is too cold for life
Excess CO2 from human activity is what causes harmful global warming

questions.q: On a day the ground is at 30 C, show that the air at 8 km in the troposphere cannot be at 25 C, and find what the temperature is likely to be.
questions.a: The temperature falls about 6.5 C per km in the troposphere, so at 8 km the fall is 52 C, giving about -22 C. 25 C would need no fall at all.
s: Temperature decreases with height at about 6.5 C per km in the troposphere
Fall over 8 km = 6.5 x 8 = 52 C, so air cannot be warmer than the ground
Likely temperature 30 - 52 = -22 C

questions.q: Explain why Venus is hotter than Mercury, and say what this warns us about Earth.
questions.a: Venus has an atmosphere that traps far more heat in an uncontrolled greenhouse effect, though Mercury is closer to the Sun. Excess CO2 from human activities strengthens Earth's greenhouse effect and, if unchecked, could make Earth uninhabitable.
s: Venus's atmosphere causes an uncontrolled greenhouse effect, though Mercury is closer
Heat trapping, not distance alone, decides the temperature
Excess CO2 on Earth could lead to dangerous global warming

questions.q: Compare the troposphere and the stratosphere under these heads: height range, how the temperature changes with height, the reason for that change and what happens as a result for the weather.
questions.a: Troposphere 0-12 km: temperature falls about 6.5 C per km because it is heated from the surface; warm air rises, driving winds and storms. Stratosphere 12-50 km: ozone absorbs UV, so temperature rises with height, which calms the layer and confines weather to the troposphere.
s: Troposphere 0-12 km; stratosphere 12-50 km
Troposphere: temperature falls about 6.5 C per km as it is heated from the surface
Rising warm air drives winds and storms in the troposphere
Stratosphere: ozone absorbs UV so temperature rises with height
This calms the stratosphere and confines weather to the troposphere

questions.q: Explain the greenhouse effect from sunlight reaching the surface to heat escaping, say why it is needed for life, and why an increase in CO2 is a problem.
questions.a: The surface absorbs sunlight and re-radiates it as infrared; greenhouse gases CO2, methane and water vapour absorb part of this heat and stop it escaping, keeping the Earth warm enough for life. Excess CO2 from human activity traps more heat, causing global warming that could make the Earth uninhabitable.
s: Surface absorbs sunlight and re-radiates it in the infrared
CO2, CH4 and water vapour absorb this heat
This prevents it escaping to space, keeping Earth warm enough for life
Excess CO2 from human activity enhances the effect
Result is global warming, which unchecked could make Earth uninhabitable

questions.q:
In 1934 K.R. Ramanathan climbed to 18000 feet in the Himalayas to measure ozone. A modern team plans the same climb on a day when the valley base is at 30 C. Take 1 foot = 0.3048 m and the troposphere's fall of 6.5 C per km. Overnight the camp is about 15 C colder than midday. Sleeping bags rated to -10 C weigh 1.2 kg each and bags rated to -25 C weigh 2.5 kg each.
(a) Convert 18000 feet to kilometres.
(b) Find the midday temperature at that height.
(c) Find the overnight camp temperature and the height still left to the top of the troposphere (12 km).
(d) Which bags should the team carry, and why?
questions.a: (a) 5.486 km. (b) 30 - 6.5 x 5.486 = -5.7 C. (c) About -20.7 C overnight; 12 - 5.486 = 6.51 km to go. (d) -25 C bags: -20.7 C is far below the -10 C rating, so the extra 1.3 kg per person is worth it for safety.
s: Part (b): about -5.7 C
Part (c): about -20.7 C and 6.51 km
Part (d): a justified choice that uses the computed temperature and the extra weight

questions.q:
A town of 500 old refrigerators is to be scrapped. Each holds 0.15 kg of CFC. If vented, the CFC reaches the sky; recovering it costs Rs 300 per refrigerator. The town budget is Rs 90000, and a state subsidy may arrive only next year.
(a) Find the total CFC in all refrigerators.
(b) Find the cost of recovering all of it.
(c) State what CFCs do to the ozone layer and what that does to the UV reaching the ground.
(d) With Rs 90000, find how much CFC is recovered and how much vented, and advise whether the town should scrap now or wait for the subsidy.
questions.a: (a) 500 x 0.15 = 75 kg. (b) Rs 1.5 lakh. (c) CFCs destroy ozone faster than it forms, thinning the layer, so more UV reaches the Earth. (d) 300 refrigerators recovered (45 kg) and 200 vented (30 kg); a justified choice, e.g. wait for the subsidy or recover 300 now and store the other 200 unvented, since venting harms the ozone layer.
s: Part (a): 75 kg
Part (b): Rs 150000
Part (c): ozone destroyed faster than formed, more UV reaches the ground
Part (d): 45 kg recovered and 30 kg vented, with a justified decision

questions.q: At 2 pm in a Himalayan valley the sun-facing slope is warm and its air is rising. The cooler air that moves up to replace it is called a ___ breeze.
questions.a: valley

questions.q: At 10 pm a hiker in a Himalayan valley near Dehradun feels cool air flowing down the slopes. Which explanation fits the chapter?
questions.a: The slopes lose heat faster than the valley floor, and the cooler, denser air flows down into the valley. This night-time flow is the mountain breeze.
o: The slopes lose heat faster than the valley floor, and the cooler, denser air flows down into the valley
The slopes have heated more than the valley floor, so warm air is falling into the valley
The valley floor has cooled faster than the slopes, so air is flowing up the slopes
Planetary winds from the equator blow down every mountain at night

questions.q: A large patch of floating plastic is carried by a gyre in the Southern Hemisphere. In which sense does it circulate?
questions.a: Counter-clockwise. Earth's rotation deflects ocean currents into gyres that run counter-clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Northern.
o: Counter-clockwise
Clockwise
Straight from the equator to the pole
Back and forth between day and night, like the valley breeze

questions.q: Which of these does the chapter NOT list as influencing the movement of ocean water?
questions.a: The number of earthquakes under the sea floor. The chapter names winds, temperature and salinity differences, rotation of the Earth and land masses.
o: The number of earthquakes under the sea floor
Strong planetary winds dragging the surface water
Differences in temperature and salinity
The rotation of the Earth and the distribution of land masses

questions.q: A port on the north-western coast of Europe, at a high latitude, stays free of ice in winter. What does the chapter give as the reason?
questions.a: The North Atlantic Drift, an extension of the Gulf Stream, brings warm water towards the coast. Ocean currents carry heat from the equator towards the poles and moderate the climate.
o: The North Atlantic Drift, an extension of the Gulf Stream, brings warm water towards the coast
Cold water from the poles keeps the coast free of ice
The port has a very high albedo and reflects all the cold
A mountain breeze blows warm air down the coast every night

questions.q: Air warmed at the equator rises and moves towards the poles at height. Where does it sink after cooling, and what forms there?
questions.a: Around 30 degrees N and S, forming sub-tropical high pressure belts. Cool, dense air sinks near 30 degrees and then flows back along the surface.
o: Around 30 degrees N and S, forming sub-tropical high pressure belts
Around 60 degrees N and S, forming sub-polar high pressure belts
At 90 degrees N and S, forming low pressure belts
At the equator again, forming an equatorial high pressure belt

questions.q:
Statement 1: Intense heating at the equator forms an equatorial low pressure belt.
Statement 2: Colder, denser water slowly flows back towards the equator at deeper ocean levels.
Statement 3: Water of lower salinity, being less dense, stays near the surface.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: All three statements. All three come directly from the sections on planetary winds and ocean currents.
o: All three statements
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Ocean currents flow only in the direction in which the wind blows over them.
Reason (R): Differences in temperature and salinity, Earth's rotation and land masses also influence ocean currents.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true. Winds drag surface water, but the other factors bend and redirect the flow, so the word 'only' makes A false.
o: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

questions.q:
Match each latitude (column I) with the pressure belt formed there (column II).
Column I: 1. Equator  2. About 30 degrees N and S  3. About 60 degrees N and S  4. About 90 degrees N and S
Column II: a. sub-tropical high  b. polar high  c. equatorial low  d. sub-polar low
questions.a: 1-c, 2-a, 3-d, 4-b. Warm air rises at the equator, sinks near 30 degrees, rises again near 60 degrees, and very cold air sinks at the poles.

questions.q:
(a) Explain why the valley breeze blows up the slopes during the day.
(b) Explain why the flow reverses after sunset.
questions.a: (a) Sun-facing slopes heat faster, the air over them warms and rises, creating low pressure, and cooler valley air moves up. (b) After sunset the slopes cool faster and the cooler, denser air flows down into the valley as a mountain breeze.
s: Part (a): slopes heat faster, warm air rises and cooler valley air replaces it
Part (b): slopes cool faster, dense cool air flows down into the valley

questions.q: True or False? Ocean currents move only at the surface of the sea. Give the verdict and the correction.
questions.a: False. Warm surface water travels towards the poles while colder, denser water flows back towards the equator at deeper levels, and higher-salinity dense water sinks and moves at depth.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: colder, denser water also flows at deeper levels towards the equator

questions.q:
A water mass in an ocean current moves at 0.5 m per second.
(a) Find the distance it covers in one day.
(b) Find the number of days it needs to travel 4320 km.
s: Part (a): 43.2 km a day
Part (b): 100 days

questions.q: Planetary winds do not blow straight from high to low pressure. State what bends them and the direction of the bending in each hemisphere.
questions.a: The rotation of the Earth deflects them: towards the right in the Northern Hemisphere and towards the left in the Southern Hemisphere.
s: The rotation of the Earth deflects the winds
Right in the Northern Hemisphere and left in the Southern Hemisphere

questions.q: Give one way in which ocean currents regulate the climate and one way in which they support ecosystems.
questions.a: They carry heat from the equator towards the poles, reducing temperature differences; they transport nutrients that support a massive ecosystem.
s: Transport heat from the equator to the poles, reducing temperature differences
Transport nutrients that support ecosystems

questions.q: Rohan says, 'Wind is caused by the rotation of the Earth.' Is he right?
questions.a: No. Wind is air moving from high to low pressure, and the pressure differences are caused mainly by the uneven heating of the surface by the Sun. The rotation of the Earth only deflects the moving air.
s: Verdict: not right
Wind is air flowing from high to low pressure caused by uneven heating
Rotation only bends the path of winds

questions.q: A cargo port at a high latitude on the north-western coast of Europe is open all winter. Working backwards, name the likely cause, where the water comes from and what it does to the climate.
questions.a: A warm current, the North Atlantic Drift (an extension of the Gulf Stream), brings warm water from low latitudes and moderates the coastal climate, keeping the port ice-free.
s: A warm ocean current such as the North Atlantic Drift
The water comes from the warmer south, carrying equatorial heat
It moderates the climate and keeps the port ice-free

questions.q: Explain how the direction of the breeze in a mountain valley changes between day and night, naming each breeze and the cause.
questions.a: By day sun-facing slopes warm quickly, air rises and cooler valley air moves up the slopes (valley breeze). By night the slopes cool faster than the valley floor and cooler, denser air flows down (mountain breeze).
s: Day: slopes warm faster and the air rises, so valley breeze
Night: slopes cool faster, so cooler denser air sinks down, giving the mountain breeze
Cause: uneven rates of heating and cooling

questions.q: Describe the circulation of air between the equator and the poles, naming each pressure belt and its latitude, and say how the Earth's rotation changes the path of the winds.
questions.a: Intense heating forms an equatorial low; the air rises, moves poleward at height, cools and sinks around 30 degrees N and S (sub-tropical high) and flows back to the equator. Part of it moves poleward and rises near 60 degrees (sub-polar low). At 90 degrees very cold air sinks (polar high). Rotation deflects the winds right in the north and left in the south.
s: Equatorial low: intense heating makes warm air rise
Air cools and sinks near 30 degrees N and S, forming the sub-tropical high
Surface air returns to the equator, while part moves poleward and rises near 60 degrees (sub-polar low)
Very cold air sinks at about 90 degrees, forming the polar high
Earth's rotation deflects the winds right in the Northern and left in the Southern Hemisphere

questions.q: List the factors that drive ocean currents and explain how each acts, including the role of continents and the formation of gyres.
questions.a: Planetary winds drag surface water by friction; differences in temperature and salinity make warm water travel on the surface and cold dense water flow at depth; the rotation of the Earth deflects the water into gyres, clockwise in the north and counter-clockwise in the south; continents block and redirect currents.
s: Planetary winds drag surface water by friction
Temperature differences: warm surface water to the poles, cold dense water at depth to the equator
Salinity differences: less salty water stays near the surface and denser, saltier water sinks
Rotation of the Earth forms gyres, clockwise in the north and counter-clockwise in the south
Continents block and redirect currents

questions.q:
A hill-school trek camps in a Himalayan valley. The air temperature at 2 pm is 28 C on the sun-facing slope and 22 C on the valley floor. At 10 pm it is 9 C on the slope and 14 C on the valley floor. The leader must choose between pitching tents on the slope, which the cool night air runs down from, or on the valley floor, where that air flows to.
(a) Find the temperature difference between slope and valley at 2 pm and at 10 pm.
(b) Name the breeze at each of these two times and its direction.
(c) Explain the cause of the reversal in terms of heating and cooling.
(d) Which site would you choose for the night, and why?
questions.a: (a) 6 C (slope warmer) at 2 pm and 5 C (valley warmer) at 10 pm. (b) Valley breeze up the slope at 2 pm; mountain breeze down the slope at 10 pm. (c) Slopes heat and cool faster than the valley floor. (d) A justified choice: the valley floor is 5 C warmer but the cool air flows down to it; the slope is colder but the flow starts there.
s: Part (a): 6 C and 5 C, with the warmer place named each time
Part (b): valley breeze up at 2 pm and mountain breeze down at 10 pm
Part (c): slopes warm and cool faster than the valley floor
Part (d): a justified site that weighs the 5 C difference against the downslope flow

questions.q:
A shipping firm handles 90000 tonnes of cargo a month at Port A on the north-western coast of Europe, which is ice-free for all 12 months because of the North Atlantic Drift. Port B, at a similar latitude on an icy coast with no warm current, is open only 8 months a year and also handles 90000 tonnes in each open month. The firm earns Rs 800 per tonne.
(a) Find the yearly cargo through each port.
(b) Find the difference in earnings between the two ports in crore rupees (1 crore = 10^7).
(c) Name the cause of Port A's advantage.
(d) The firm can buy an icebreaker for Port B or move all its trade to Port A. Which would you advise, and what risk is there in relying on a current?
questions.a: (a) 1080000 t and 720000 t. (b) 360000 x 800 = Rs 28.8 crore. (c) The North Atlantic Drift carries warm water to the coast and keeps it ice-free. (d) A justified plan, e.g. move trade to A and keep B as a spare; the risk is that the current, and so the warmth, may change with climate.
s: Part (a): 1080000 tonnes and 720000 tonnes
Part (b): Rs 28.8 crore
Part (c): warm North Atlantic Drift keeps the coast ice-free
Part (d): a justified choice that includes the risk of depending on a current

questions.q: A 200 kg dry sample of plant material is about 49% carbon, so it holds ___ kg of carbon.
A farmer grows groundnut, a legume, and finds that it needs far less nitrogen fertiliser than wheat. Which process in the root nodules explains this?
questions.a: Rhizobium bacteria convert atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia. Nitrogen fixation by Rhizobium gives the plant a supply of usable nitrogen compounds.
o: Rhizobium bacteria convert atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia
Nitrobacter in the nodules turns ammonia into nitrogen gas
Pseudomonas in the nodules fixes nitrogen gas into nitrate
Decomposers in the nodules release oxygen for the plant to use

questions.q: Which pairing of bacteria and their role in the nitrogen cycle is correct?
questions.a: Nitrosomonas turns ammonia into nitrite and Nitrobacter turns nitrite into nitrate. Together the two steps make up nitrification.
o: Nitrosomonas turns ammonia into nitrite and Nitrobacter turns nitrite into nitrate
Nitrosomonas turns nitrite into nitrate and Nitrobacter turns ammonia into nitrite
Nitrosomonas turns nitrate into nitrogen gas and Nitrobacter fixes nitrogen gas
Nitrosomonas fixes nitrogen gas and Nitrobacter turns nitrate into ammonia

questions.q: Which statement about carbon on Earth is NOT correct?
questions.a: The atmosphere holds most of Earth's carbon, about 71%. It is the oceans, not the atmosphere, that hold about 71% of the carbon.
o: The atmosphere holds most of Earth's carbon, about 71%
About 71% of global carbon is found in the oceans
The atmosphere holds only about 1% of global carbon
Carbon is about 49% of the dry weight of living organisms

questions.q: A bonfire burns, a runner pants and a banyan tree stands in the sun. Which of these three restores the oxygen used by the others?
questions.a: The banyan tree, through photosynthesis. Combustion and respiration use up oxygen and release CO2; photosynthesis restores the oxygen.
o: The banyan tree, through photosynthesis
The bonfire, because burning forms oxygen from fuel
The runner, because breathing out returns oxygen to the air
All three equally, because each exchanges gases with the air

questions.q:
Statement 1: Ammonification is the change of nitrite into nitrate by Nitrobacter.
Statement 2: Plants and animals can use nitrogen gas directly from the air.
Statement 3: The Haber-Bosch process makes ammonia from atmospheric nitrogen for fertilisers.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 3 only. Statement 1 describes nitrification, and statement 2 is false because nitrogen gas is non-reactive and must first be converted to soluble compounds.
o: Statement 3 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Keeling curve of atmospheric CO2 has a sawtooth pattern.
Reason (R): Yearly plant growth in the Northern Hemisphere absorbs CO2 and causes seasonal dips.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. The dips repeat every year as plants grow, on top of a rising trend.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
Match each bacterium (column I) with its role (column II).
Column I: 1. Rhizobium  2. Nitrosomonas  3. Nitrobacter  4. Pseudomonas
Column II: a. nitrite to nitrate  b. fixes N2 to ammonia in legume root nodules  c. ammonia to nitrite  d. nitrate back to nitrogen gas
questions.a: 1-b, 2-c, 3-a, 4-d. Rhizobium fixes, Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter nitrify in two steps and Pseudomonas denitrifies.

questions.q:
(a) State the time scales of the fast and the slow carbon cycles.
(b) Name one process in each.
questions.a: (a) Fast: days to years; slow: millions of years. (b) Fast: photosynthesis or respiration or decomposition; slow: formation of fossil fuels from buried dead organisms.
s: Part (a): days to years and millions of years
Part (b): one process each, e.g. photosynthesis and fossil fuel formation

questions.q: True or False? The oxygen used up by respiration and combustion is restored mainly by photosynthesis. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Plants use sunlight, water and CO2 in photosynthesis to form glucose and release oxygen, balancing the consumption.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: photosynthesis releases O2 and balances respiration and combustion

questions.q:
Atmospheric CO2 rose from 315 ppm in 1960 to 420 ppm in 2025.
(a) Find the rise and the average rise per year, to one decimal place.
(b) If the rise continued at this rate, find the CO2 level in 2045, to the nearest ppm.
questions.a: (a) 105 ppm; 105/65 = 1.6 ppm per year. (b) 420 + 20 x 1.615 = about 452 ppm.
s: Part (a): 105 ppm and about 1.6 ppm per year
Part (b): about 452 ppm

questions.q: State how a warmer atmosphere changes rainfall and how heavy bursts of rain affect groundwater.
questions.a: A warmer atmosphere holds more moisture, so some areas get heavier rain and others drought. Sudden intense rain gives more run-off and less infiltration, which reduces groundwater recharge.
s: Warmer air holds more moisture: heavier rain in some areas and drought elsewhere
More run-off, less infiltration, so less groundwater recharge

questions.q: Name the process in which decomposers return nitrogen compounds to the soil, and the process in which nitrate is turned back into nitrogen gas, with a bacterium for the second.
questions.a: Ammonification; denitrification by Pseudomonas.
s: Ammonification returns ammonia to the soil
Denitrification by Pseudomonas converts nitrate to nitrogen gas

questions.q: Amit says, 'The atmosphere is the biggest store of carbon, which is why CO2 is such a big problem.' Is he right?
questions.a: No. The oceans hold about 71% of the world's carbon, while the atmosphere holds only about 1%. Because the atmospheric store is so small, the added CO2 changes it by a large fraction.
s: Verdict: not right
Oceans hold about 71% and the atmosphere only about 1%
A small store changes noticeably when extra carbon is added

questions.q: Show that burning fuel cannot be the process that restores the oxygen in the air, and name the process that does.
questions.a: Combustion of fuels uses oxygen and releases CO2, so it lowers the oxygen level. Only photosynthesis releases O2, using sunlight, water and CO2.
s: Combustion uses oxygen
It releases CO2, so it cannot restore oxygen
Photosynthesis restores O2 using sunlight, water and CO2

questions.q: A pea field needs much less nitrogen fertiliser than a wheat field. Working backwards, state the reason and name the process, the bacterium and the part of the plant.
questions.a: Peas are legumes whose root nodules house Rhizobium. The bacteria carry out nitrogen fixation, turning atmospheric N2 into ammonia the plant can use.
s: Pea is a legume with root nodules
Rhizobium fixes atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia
So the plant has its own usable nitrogen and needs less fertiliser

questions.q: Starting with a plant using CO2, trace the carbon through the fast cycle and the slow cycle until it returns to the atmosphere, naming each process.
questions.a: Plants take in CO2 and make glucose by photosynthesis; respiration returns CO2; animals eat plants and, when organisms die, decomposition returns CO2. In the slow cycle dead organisms are buried and become coal, oil and gas over millions of years; burning these fuels releases CO2 quickly.
s: Photosynthesis turns atmospheric CO2 into glucose
Respiration releases CO2 back to the air
Animals eat plants; death and decomposition return CO2
Slow cycle: buried organisms become coal, oil and gas over millions of years
Burning fossil fuels releases the carbon as CO2 in a very short time

questions.q: Describe the five steps of the nitrogen cycle in order, naming a bacterium where the chapter gives one, and explain why nitrogen gas must be changed before living things can use it.
questions.a: N2 is non-reactive and must first become soluble compounds. Fixation by Rhizobium or Azotobacter makes ammonia; nitrification by Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter makes nitrite then nitrate; plants assimilate these and animals eat plants; decomposers carry out ammonification; denitrification by Pseudomonas returns N2 to the air.
s: N2 is non-reactive and cannot be used directly, so it needs conversion
Fixation to ammonia by Rhizobium or Azotobacter
Nitrification: ammonia to nitrite (Nitrosomonas) to nitrate (Nitrobacter)
Assimilation by plants and ammonification by decomposers
Denitrification by Pseudomonas returns N2 to the air

questions.q:
A farmer has 5 hectares. Wheat needs 120 kg of nitrogen per hectare from urea; chickpea, a legume, needs only 20 kg per hectare. Urea is 46% nitrogen and costs Rs 6 per kg. A hectare of wheat earns Rs 52000 and a hectare of chickpea Rs 45000.
(a) Find the urea needed for one hectare of wheat, to the nearest kg.
(b) Find the fertiliser bill if all 5 hectares are wheat.
(c) Name the process that lets chickpea manage with little urea.
(d) The farmer considers 3 hectares of wheat and 2 of chickpea. Find the saving in fertiliser cost and the loss in earnings, and advise whether it is worth it, mentioning one environmental benefit.
questions.a: (a) 120/0.46 = 261 kg. (b) 5 x 260.87 x 6 = about Rs 7826. (c) Nitrogen fixation by Rhizobium. (d) The bill falls to about Rs 5218, a saving of about Rs 2609, but earnings fall by 2 x 7000 = Rs 14000; so the mix loses money on these figures. Less fertiliser lowers the risk of eutrophication, so it is worth it only if the farm values soil and water, or the legume sells at a better price.
s: Part (b): about Rs 7826
Part (c): nitrogen fixation by Rhizobium in root nodules
Part (d): saving about Rs 2609, loss Rs 14000, with a justified decision and an environmental benefit

questions.q:
As a model, take the world's carbon as 100 units, with 71 in the oceans and 1 in the atmosphere. Suppose burning fossil fuels adds 0.5 unit to the atmosphere. The ocean then absorbs 0.3 unit of that, but the chapter warns this makes the sea water more acidic.
(a) Find the percentage rise in atmospheric carbon if none were absorbed.
(b) Find the percentage rise after the ocean absorbs its 0.3 unit.
(c) Name two organisms or systems threatened by the more acidic sea water.
(d) A government can rely on the oceans to absorb the rest, or plant forests and cut fossil fuel use. Which would you advise, and why?
questions.a: (a) 0.5/1 = 50%. (b) (0.5 - 0.3)/1 = 20%. (c) Plankton and coral reefs. (d) A justified choice, e.g. cut fossil fuel use and plant forests, because the ocean absorption acidifies the water and warmer oceans absorb CO2 less well as a sink.
s: Part (a): 50%
Part (b): 20%
Part (c): plankton and coral reefs
Part (d): a justified choice that notes the limits of the ocean as a sink

questions.q: Heavy use of nitrogen fertiliser on a farm washes nitrate into a lake, causing an algal bloom, a fall in oxygen and the death of fish. This process is called ___.
questions.a: eutrophication

questions.q: Fishermen at a lake find many dead fish after algae turned the water green. Which chain does the chapter support?
questions.a: Excess nitrate from fertiliser, algal bloom, oxygen depleted, fish die. This is eutrophication, which threatens water bodies and coastal fisheries.
o: Excess nitrate from fertiliser, algal bloom, oxygen depleted, fish die
Excess phosphate from soil, fewer algae, more oxygen, fish multiply
Excess CO2 from the air, warm water, algae die, fish die of hunger
Excess nitrate from fertiliser, plants absorb it, oxygen rises, fish die of heat

questions.q: A hill slope that supplies a village is cleared of its forest. Which set of effects does the chapter predict?
questions.a: Less photosynthesis and transpiration, lower local rainfall, changed albedo, more soil erosion. Without trees there is less transpiration, the soil is no longer held by roots and habitats are lost.
o: Less photosynthesis and transpiration, lower local rainfall, changed albedo, more soil erosion
More transpiration, higher local rainfall, unchanged albedo, less soil erosion
Less photosynthesis, higher local rainfall, more soil held by roots
No change in rainfall, but a gain in biodiversity as new species move in

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an effect of excess atmospheric CO2 described in the chapter?
questions.a: Sea water becomes more alkaline, which protects plankton and coral reefs. Extra CO2 makes sea water more acidic, which threatens plankton and coral reefs.
o: Sea water becomes more alkaline, which protects plankton and coral reefs
Sea water becomes more acidic
The greenhouse effect is intensified
Warmer oceans absorb CO2 less effectively as a carbon sink

questions.q: What does the chapter conclude from comparing the Montreal Protocol with the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement?
questions.a: Global cooperation has begun to restore the ozone layer but has been less successful on CO2 emissions. The ozone layer is slowly recovering, whereas the CO2 agreements have been less successful.
o: Global cooperation has begun to restore the ozone layer but has been less successful on CO2 emissions
All three agreements reduced emissions equally well
Global cooperation cannot work, so only individuals can help
The Montreal Protocol was about CO2 and failed, while Kyoto and Paris succeeded

questions.q:
Statement 1: Deforestation increases photosynthesis and transpiration, which raises local rainfall.
Statement 2: The overuse of fertilisers has degraded soil and water although the Haber-Bosch process helped India's Green Revolution.
Statement 3: The Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement are the successful agreements that are helping the ozone layer recover.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 2 only. Statement 1 is false because deforestation lowers photosynthesis and transpiration; statement 3 is false because the Montreal Protocol, not Kyoto or Paris, helps the ozone layer.
o: Statement 2 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Haber-Bosch process helped India's Green Revolution and feeds billions.
Reason (R): The Haber-Bosch reaction is energy intensive and uses about 1-2% of global energy.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. The process makes ammonia for fertilisers (A), and its energy use is an additional cost, not the reason for its benefits.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: A school starts a drive in which pupils switch off lights, carry water bottles, plant saplings and recycle waste. Which Indian initiative, introduced at a UN climate conference in 2021, matches this spirit?
questions.a: Mission LiFE (Lifestyle for Environment). Mission LiFE encourages mindful, eco-friendly lifestyles.
o: Mission LiFE (Lifestyle for Environment)
The Montreal Protocol
The Kyoto Protocol
The Haber-Bosch process

questions.q:
(a) State what extra atmospheric CO2 does to sea water.
(b) Name two kinds of living things that this threatens.
questions.a: (a) It makes the sea water more acidic. (b) Plankton and coral reefs.
s: Part (a): sea water becomes more acidic
Part (b): plankton and coral reefs

questions.q: True or False? A warmer ocean becomes a weaker carbon sink. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Warmer ocean water absorbs CO2 less effectively, so more CO2 stays in the atmosphere and adds to warming.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: warmer water has a reduced capacity to absorb CO2

questions.q:
A farmer in a river catchment applies 180 kg of nitrogen per hectare on 12 hectares, and 30% of it washes into the river.
(a) Find the nitrogen reaching the river.
(b) Find the nitrogen applied if the farmer cuts the application by 25%.
s: Part (a): 648 kg
Part (b): 1620 kg

questions.q: Give two effects of deforestation, one on local rainfall and one on the soil.
questions.a: Fewer trees mean less photosynthesis and transpiration, which can reduce local rainfall; without roots to hold the soil, erosion increases.
s: Less transpiration and photosynthesis can lower local rainfall
Soil erosion increases without roots to hold the soil

questions.q: Distinguish the ozone found high in the stratosphere from the ozone found near the ground in cities.
questions.a: Stratospheric ozone blocks UV radiation and protects life. Ground-level ozone is formed when vehicle emissions react with sunlight, and it is harmful to health.
s: Stratospheric ozone is protective because it blocks UV
Ground-level ozone forms from vehicle emissions and sunlight and is harmful

questions.q: Tanvi says, 'The Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement have worked as well as the Montreal Protocol.' Is she right?
questions.a: No. The Montreal Protocol has started the recovery of the ozone layer, but the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement, meant to reduce CO2 emissions, have been less successful.
s: Verdict: not right
Montreal Protocol has started the recovery of the ozone layer
Kyoto and Paris on CO2 emissions have been less successful

questions.q: A lake in a farming district turns green and its fish die. Working backwards, name the likely human cause, the process and what removes the fish.
questions.a: Overuse of fertiliser adds excess nitrate to the lake. This causes eutrophication, an algal bloom, and the algae deplete oxygen, so the fish die.
s: Overuse of fertiliser adds excess nitrate
Algal bloom through eutrophication
Depleted oxygen kills the fish

questions.q: Suggest three actions, one by a government or the world, one by a community and one by an individual, that the chapter says can help restore the balance of the Earth's systems.
questions.a: World: global cooperation or a shift to renewable energy such as solar and wind. Community: planting trees or sustainable farming. Individual: reducing waste, reusing, recycling and saving water, food and energy.
s: A global or national action, e.g. renewable energy or international agreement
A community action, e.g. planting trees or sustainable farming
An individual action, e.g. saving resources, reduce, reuse, recycle

questions.q: Explain the effects of deforestation on the water, the carbon and the oxygen cycles and on soil and living things, in five distinct points.
questions.a: Fewer trees mean less photosynthesis, so less CO2 is taken up and less oxygen is released; transpiration falls and local rainfall may decline; albedo of the surface changes; without roots the soil erodes more; habitats are destroyed and biodiversity declines.
s: Less photosynthesis: less CO2 taken in and less O2 released
Less transpiration, so local rainfall may fall
Surface albedo is altered
Soil erosion increases without roots
Habitat loss leads to decline in biodiversity

questions.q: Discuss how the ozone layer's recovery and the stalled progress on CO2 differ, and what actions at the world, national, community and individual levels the chapter says can help.
questions.a: CFCs from refrigerators and aerosols thinned the ozone layer; the Montreal Protocol cut CFC use and the layer is slowly recovering. The Kyoto Protocol and Paris Agreement on CO2 have been less successful. Actions: renewable energy, planting trees, saving water, sustainable farming; individuals reduce, reuse, recycle, as promoted by Mission LiFE.
s: CFCs caused the ozone hole
Montreal Protocol reduced CFC use and the layer is slowly recovering
Kyoto and Paris on CO2 emissions have been less successful
Restoration actions: renewable energy, planting trees, saving water, sustainable farming
Individual actions: reduce, reuse, recycle, and Mission LiFE

questions.q:
A lake supports 50 fishing families. Since farms around it began using more fertiliser, the daily catch has fallen from 400 kg to 150 kg, and fish sell at Rs 120 per kg. The fishermen work 300 days a year. A subsidy scheme costing Rs 1.5 crore would train farmers in careful fertiliser use.
(a) Find the daily fall in income of the fishing community and the loss per family per day.
(b) Find the yearly loss.
(c) Name the process behind the fall in the catch.
(d) Should the district spend Rs 1.5 crore on the scheme or simply compensate the fishermen each year? Justify using your figures.
questions.a: (a) 250 x 120 = Rs 30000 a day; Rs 600 per family. (b) 30000 x 300 = Rs 90 lakh. (c) Eutrophication from excess nitrate. (d) The scheme costs about 1.67 years of the loss; a justified choice, e.g. fund the scheme because compensation never ends and the lake keeps degrading.
s: Part (a): Rs 30000 a day and Rs 600 per family
Part (b): Rs 90 lakh a year
Part (c): eutrophication caused by excess nitrate
Part (d): a justified choice using the payback of about 1.67 years

questions.q:
A village with 600 hectares of forest and 300 hectares of farm plans to clear 150 hectares of forest for new farms. New land would earn Rs 40000 per hectare a year. Experts expect local rainfall to fall by 10% (from 1200 mm), which would reduce yields on the existing 300 hectares, earning Rs 60000 per hectare, by 8%.
(a) Find the new rainfall.
(b) Find the yearly income from the new farms.
(c) Find the yearly loss on the old farms.
(d) The village can clear 150 hectares or clear 75 hectares and expect half the rainfall effect. Which would you recommend, and what other costs should be counted?
questions.a: (a) 1080 mm. (b) 150 x 40000 = Rs 60 lakh. (c) 300 x 60000 x 0.08 = Rs 14.4 lakh. (d) Clearing 150 ha nets Rs 45.6 lakh and 75 ha nets Rs 22.8 lakh in income; a justified choice that also counts soil erosion, albedo change and loss of biodiversity, which have no money figure here.
s: Part (b): Rs 60 lakh
Part (c): Rs 14.4 lakh
Part (d): net incomes Rs 45.6 lakh and Rs 22.8 lakh and a justified choice that counts erosion, albedo and biodiversity
